title: Who should pay for the ageing population?

turns.speaker: Mei
turns.text: The ratio is the thing that gets me. Four working-age people per pensioner now, and about two by the middle of the century.

turns.speaker: Idris
turns.text: And the pension is paid out of today's taxes, not out of anything anyone saved.

turns.speaker: Gwen
turns.text: Which people genuinely don't know. They think there's a pot with their name on it.

turns.speaker: Mei
turns.text: So the options are the usual three. Work longer, pay more, or get less.

turns.speaker: Idris
turns.text: Work longer is the one that sounds painless and isn't. Life expectancy went up, but healthy life expectancy barely moved, and it's very uneven.

turns.speaker: Gwen
turns.text: Meaning a manual worker gets a shorter retirement and a worse one.

turns.speaker: Idris
turns.text: Considerably. Raising the age by a year takes more from them than from an accountant.

turns.speaker: Mei
turns.text: You could vary it by career length rather than by age, which a few countries have tried.

turns.speaker: Gwen
turns.text: Immigration is the other lever and nobody wants to say it out loud in a manifesto.

turns.speaker: Idris
turns.text: It buys time rather than solving it. Migrants also get old.

turns.speaker: Gwen
turns.text: True, but time is exactly what you need to adjust the rest of it gradually.

turns.speaker: Mei
turns.text: The part I find honest is admitting none of this is a crisis that arrived. We've known the numbers for forty years.

turns.speaker: Idris
turns.text: Which makes it a choice rather than a shock.

points: The ratio of working-age people to pensioners falls from about four to about two by mid-century.
Pensions are funded from current taxation rather than individual savings, which many people misunderstand.
The three options are working longer, paying more, or receiving less.
Idris argues raising the pension age is regressive, since healthy life expectancy has barely risen and varies sharply by occupation.
Mei suggests varying entitlement by career length rather than age.
Immigration is acknowledged as a lever that buys time rather than solving the problem, and they conclude the situation is a long-known choice rather than a sudden crisis.
